regions.name: Middle East
overview: The Yemen war has turned into an open Saudi-led counter-offensive: on 4 October the government launched Operation Yemen Dawn, backed by about 100 Saudi jets, and claimed to have retaken Mokha, Dhubab airport and the Bab al-Mandeb shoreline (not independently verified). The Houthis answered on 6–7 October with missiles that hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha airport, killing 3 and wounding 36. The WHO now counts 959 dead and more than 5,000 casualties since 6 August.

The US–Iran confrontation is still stuck between a stalled diplomatic track and continuing coercion at sea. After the Witkoff–Araghchi contact at the UN, President Pezeshkian called talks 'meaningless' on 5 October. At least four tankers were hit by unidentified projectiles near Hormuz and off Qatar between 4 and 7 October, and IRGC-linked media claimed 13 'violator' tankers were targeted in a week. No US or Israeli strikes on Iranian territory were found in open sources this week.

The US exit from Iraq was completed on 30 September without disarming the hardline militias. Kataib Hezbollah suspended military operations and declared that 'the resistance has won this round', while five militias reportedly accepted a 30 June 2027 deadline to hand weapons to the state. Islamic State moved quickly to test the post-US security gap, with deadly attacks near Kirkuk and in Nineveh on 4–5 October.

Israel kept up a steady tempo of operations on its periphery around the third anniversary of 7 October and ahead of the 27 October election. It carried out deadly strikes in Gaza (1,446 killed since the October 2025 ceasefire), shelled and launched drone strikes on south Lebanon almost every day, and made weekly tank-supported incursions into Quneitra and Daraa. Settler violence also rose during the West Bank olive harvest.

countries.name: Gaza
incidents: 3 Oct — Gaza City: An Israeli strike on an apartment building killed at least 5, including 4 women, two of them members of Gaza's small Christian community; the IDF said it had killed a Hamas official in an apartment used for 'terror activities'.
4 Oct — Deir al-Balah: An Israeli strike on a vehicle killed 1 Palestinian and injured 10; the toll since the October 2025 ceasefire reached 1,446 killed and more than 5,060 injured.
6–7 Oct — Gaza/Israel: Defence Minister Katz ordered all crossings into Gaza and the West Bank closed for the third anniversary of the 7 October 2023 attack.
7 Oct — Northern Gaza: An Israeli strike killed a member of the Hamas-run civil defence rescue service.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The nominal ceasefire continues to coexist with deadly Israeli strikes several times a week, increasingly framed as targeted killings of named Hamas figures in residential buildings, with civilian deaths alongside. The closure of the crossings for the 7 October anniversary shows how quickly Israel can cut off aid flows for security or political reasons. Over the next 90 days, expect this pattern of strikes on vehicles and apartments to continue through the 27 October election and the government formation that follows, with a risk of sharper escalation if attacks on IDF troops along the Yellow Line grow. A renegotiated enforcement mechanism or a substantive phase-two deal is unlikely before a new Israeli government is in place, and humanitarian conditions will stay severe as winter begins.

countries.name: Lebanon
incidents: 3 Oct — South Lebanon (Talloussah, Bani Haiyyan): Lebanese state media reported Israeli artillery shelling of the two border towns.
4 Oct — Tyre district/South Lebanon: Israeli forces shelled and struck several towns, including Mansouri, Baraachit, Kfar Tebnit and Wadi al-Hujair, according to Lebanese state media.
5–6 Oct — Bint Jbeil district (Haddatha, Baraachit, Haris): Israeli shelling hit the outskirts of Haddatha and Baraachit on consecutive days, and an Israeli drone strike hit near Haris on 6 October.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Israel is still waging a daily campaign of artillery, air and drone strikes on south Lebanon from the strip it occupies, and Hezbollah refuses to disarm. Casualty figures for this week could not be confirmed in open sources, but the pattern of strikes has not changed. The decisive factor for the next 90 days is UNIFIL's departure in January: if no European or other follow-on force is agreed, a security gap south of the Litani raises the risk of friction between the IDF and the Lebanese army, and of Israel pushing deeper. The Lebanese army's disarmament plan north of the Litani is unlikely to make real progress while strikes continue. A post-election Israeli government could re-examine the Lebanon front, but an Israeli withdrawal within this period is unlikely.

countries.name: Iran
incidents: 4–5 Oct — Strait of Hormuz: UKMTO reported three tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in two days (an LPG carrier and a crude tanker on 4 Oct, and a third on 5 Oct that caught fire in its engine room); the IRGC hailed and turned back an inbound tanker 11 nm north of Khasab, and IRGC-affiliated Fars said Iran had targeted 13 'violator' tankers in seven days.

5 Oct — Tehran: President Pezeshkian called talks with the US 'meaningless', saying Iran had been 'attacked three times' after earlier rounds of negotiations, while Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz reopening roadmap, which was tied to lifting the US naval blockade, easing sanctions and releasing frozen funds.

3 and 5 Oct — Iran: The judiciary executed three men arrested during the January protests (Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi on 3 Oct; Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raisi on 5 Oct), bringing protest-related executions to 35 since January.
7 Oct — Gulf (off Qatar): A tanker reported being hit by multiple projectiles, per the maritime security agency.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. No strikes on Iranian territory were found this week, but the war with the US has not ended. There is no ceasefire, the US naval blockade remains in place, and Iranian forces are using force at sea almost daily to keep Hormuz effectively closed, so the underlying conflict has not genuinely decreased. The diplomatic track has stalled: Pezeshkian's rejection of talks and Trump's rejection of Tehran's roadmap leave no agreed basis for negotiation, while IRGC media attacks on FM Araghchi show the hardliners setting the terms. Over the next 90 days, expect continued tanker strikes and seizures, harsh internal repression (an execution rate of almost two a week) and a substantial risk of renewed US strikes if a tanker hit causes mass casualties or the Houthi–Saudi war draws in US forces. A deal before the US midterms is unlikely.

countries.name: Yemen
incidents: 4 Oct — Nationwide: PLC chairman al-Alimi launched Operation Yemen Dawn to retake Sanaa; the army reported strikes on 1,122 Houthi targets in Saada, al-Jawf and Taiz, and the Saudi-led coalition said about 100 jets hit 324 'high-value' targets.

5 Oct — Taiz coast (Mokha/Dhubab/Bab al-Mandeb): Government forces, led by the Giants Brigades and Nation's Shield, claimed to have taken Mokha, Dhubab airport and the Bab al-Mandeb shoreline and to have cut the Dhubab–Mokha road; the claims were not independently verified or confirmed by the Houthis.

7 Oct — Western Yemen/Taiz/Aden: At least 62 combatants (37 of them Houthis) were killed in clashes; a Houthi missile wounded 5 civilians in Taiz city, and another struck near the runway of Aden International Airport, forcing a Yemenia flight to divert to Jeddah.
Early Oct — Yemen: The WHO recorded 959 deaths and more than 5,000 casualties since 6 August (685 in six days), nearly 200,000 displaced and 647 suspected cholera cases.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The conflict has escalated from a Houthi coastal offensive into a full government–Saudi counter-offensive with the declared aim of retaking Sanaa, and with explicit political backing from US Secretary of State Rubio. If confirmed, the reported recapture of Mokha and Dhubab would reverse the Houthis' September gains on Bab al-Mandeb, but those claims are unverified. Over the next 90 days, expect intense ground fighting on the west coast and in Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf, a very high tempo of Saudi air strikes with civilian casualties in Sanaa, and Houthi missile and drone fire on Saudi airports, Aden and shipping. A move on Sanaa itself is unlikely to succeed within this period. The cholera outbreak and the displacement of nearly 200,000 people point to a fast-worsening humanitarian crisis.

countries.name: Israel
incidents: 28 Sep — Jordan border: The IDF thwarted an attempt to fly 10 guns from Jordan into Israel by drone.
7 Oct — West Bank (Burqa, between Nablus and Tulkarem): Settlers attacked Palestinian olive pickers; Israeli forces then opened live fire, killing 1 Palestinian and injuring 14.

7 Oct — West Bank (Deir Nidham/Beit Duqqu/Isawiyah): Settlers torched an activist's car and sprayed graffiti against Israeli security chiefs; the IDF carried out brigade-level arrest raids and demolished the home of the gunman who killed Netanel Shukrun near Neve Tzuf on 20 September.
7 Oct — Nationwide: Israel marked the third anniversary of the 7 October attack with memorials and protests, under a closure of the Gaza and West Bank crossings.
countries.coa: HIGH (down from CRITICAL). Israel remains at war on several fronts, but almost all of the fighting this cycle took place outside its own territory, in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. No missile, drone or rocket attacks on Israel itself were found this week. Inside the country and the West Bank, the threat is recurring deadly violence: settler attacks during the olive harvest, IDF raids, and the Neve Tzuf killing and its aftermath. Over the next 90 days, the main escalation risks are a resumption of Iranian or Houthi missile fire if the US–Iran war heats up again, Hezbollah fire on the north, and a spike in West Bank violence around the 27 October election. Any renewed direct attack on Israeli territory would put the country back at CRITICAL. A Netanyahu win would likely keep the current posture on every front, while a coalition led by Eisenkot might seek an exit on Lebanon.

countries.name: Iraq
incidents: 30 Sep — Erbil: US forces left their last base, completing the withdrawal from Iraq and ending the anti-ISIS coalition's Iraq mission; Kurdish officials voiced concern about the removal of US air defences after more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks on the Kurdistan Region during the war.

1 Oct — Baghdad: Kataib Hezbollah leader Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi suspended military operations 'except against hostile aircraft' but denied any disarmament deal, saying 'the resistance has won this round'; PM al-Zaidi marked a 'Sovereignty Day'.

4 Oct — Nineveh (southern desert, north of Rawa): An ISIS-era IED killed 2 Iraqi soldiers and wounded 2 during a search operation; separately, the PM's office announced arrests over the trampling of a US flag by PMF members.

5 Oct — Kirkuk (near Hawija): ISIS fighters attacked a federal police position with machine guns and snipers, killing 1 policeman and wounding 4, the first reported ISIS attack on security forces since the US exit; on 6 Oct, five militias reportedly agreed to put their weapons under state control by 30 June 2027.
countries.coa: HIGH (down from CRITICAL). With US forces gone and Kataib Hezbollah formally suspending operations, the militia rocket and drone campaign on Iraqi soil has paused, and no attacks on the Kurdistan Region were found this week. Iraq now fits the HIGH definition rather than CRITICAL: there is recurring deadly violence, now led by ISIS testing the post-US gap, but no active armed conflict on Iraqi territory. Over the next 90 days, the main risks are a resurgence of ISIS in Kirkuk, Nineveh and Anbar, militias using Iraqi territory to launch drones at Saudi or Gulf targets in support of the Houthis, and possible Israeli strikes on militias in Iraq, which reports say are being prepared. The 30 June 2027 disarmament plan lacks interim milestones, and the hardline factions (Kataib Hezbollah, Nujaba, Ashab al-Kahf) remain outside it. A return to CRITICAL is plausible if the US–Iran war heats up again.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
incidents: 4–5 Oct — Yemen/Saudi Arabia: About 100 Royal Saudi Air Force jets joined Operation Yemen Dawn, flying round-the-clock sorties and hitting 324 'high-value' Houthi targets; the US Secretary of State endorsed Riyadh's right to self-defence.
6–7 Oct — Riyadh: A Houthi ballistic missile struck King Khalid International Airport, killing a Sudanese national; the coalition said it intercepted another Houthi ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
6–7 Oct — Abha: A Houthi attack on Abha International Airport killed an Egyptian and an Algerian national; the total from the two airport strikes was 3 dead and 36 wounded.
7 Oct — Khamis Mushait: The coalition intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the King Khalid Air Base area and struck 82 Houthi missile, command and communications targets in response.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Saudi Arabia is now a direct belligerent in an open war: its air force is leading a counter-offensive in Yemen, and Houthi missiles are hitting Saudi civilian airports, with the first confirmed deaths on Saudi soil in this escalation. Over the next 90 days, expect continued Houthi ballistic missile and drone fire on Riyadh, Abha, Jizan, Khamis Mushait and Red Sea energy sites such as Yanbu, and recurring airport disruption and civilian casualties despite high interception rates. Riyadh will push Washington for more direct support. The risk of a successful hit on energy infrastructure remains significant, and Iraqi militias could join in, as the September drone attack on the East-West pipeline launched from Maysan showed. A ceasefire is unlikely while the ground offensive continues.

countries.name: Syria
incidents: 2 Oct — Daraa (Maariya, Yarmouk Basin): An Israeli force of about 15 military vehicles entered the village at dawn from the al-Jazeera Barracks base and searched civilian homes.
2 Oct — Quneitra (al-Mantara Dam): Israeli forces shelled agricultural land around the dam.

6 Oct — Southern Quneitra (al-Dir'iyat Hill/Saida al-Golan): An Israeli force of two tanks and several vehicles pushed into al-Dir'iyat Hill near al-Muallaqah and into Saida al-Golan, while reconnaissance aircraft flew over Daraa.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Foreign forces hold and keep expanding a de facto security zone in Quneitra and western Daraa, with tank-supported incursions, home searches and shelling every week, and Suwayda remains outside effective state control after repeated deadly clashes in August and September. No new deadly Suwayda clashes were confirmed this week, but the ceasefire there remains fragile. Over the next 90 days, expect routine Israeli incursions and detentions, a risk of Israeli air strikes if Damascus moves forces south, and a renewed flare-up in Suwayda. US-mediated security talks with Israel are likely to stay stalled over the Golan.

countries.name: Egypt
incidents: Early Oct (reported 2–3 Oct) — Washington/Cairo: The US State Department waived human-rights conditions on more than $300 million in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo's 'helpful role' in the Iran war.
6–7 Oct — Abha (Saudi Arabia): An Egyptian national was among the 3 killed in the Houthi missile attacks on Saudi airports.
countries.coa: MODERATE (down from HIGH). No armed violence, terrorist attack or military incident on Egyptian territory was found this week; Egypt's exposure is economic and diplomatic. It is exposed through Suez Canal revenue and the Bab al-Mandeb fighting, through its mediator role between Washington and Tehran and on Gaza, and through political tension. Under the new definitions, being near the Yemen and Iran wars does not by itself justify HIGH. Over the next 90 days, watch for an Egyptian naval deployment to the southern Red Sea, which would make Egypt a potential Houthi target, any spillover from Gaza along the Rafah border, and Suez traffic data as the Yemeni government contests Bab al-Mandeb. US aid without conditions reinforces the government's security-first stance at home.

countries.name: Jordan
incidents: 24 Sep–8 Oct — Jordanian airspace: No Iranian missile or drone strike on Jordan was reported, extending the lull since the 9 September barrage on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base to about four weeks.
28 Sep — Jordan–Israel border: The IDF said it thwarted an attempt to fly 10 guns from Jordan into Israel by drone, highlighting continued arms smuggling across Jordanian territory.

30 Sep — Northern Iraq/Jordan: The US completed its withdrawal from Iraq, with most of the remaining troops redeploying to Jordan and other regional bases, adding to the US footprint on Jordanian soil.
countries.coa: HIGH (down from CRITICAL). Jordan suffered direct Iranian missile attacks during the summer, but no attack on its territory has been reported for about four weeks, so it no longer fits CRITICAL ('direct military attacks on the country'). The threat has not gone away: the US–Iran war is unresolved, Jordan hosts a growing concentration of US forces, and renewed Iranian barrages on Muwaffaq Salti or other bases are a credible risk. HIGH therefore reflects a real risk of military escalation, not calm. Over the next 90 days, Jordan will stay on high air-defence alert and keep up pressure on drone and weapons smuggling across its Syrian and Israeli borders. Any new Iranian strike on Jordanian soil would put it back at CRITICAL.

countries.name: Libya
incidents: 21 Sep (ongoing) — Sharara–Zawiya pipeline: Petroleum Facilities Guard personnel shut a valve on the pipeline from Libya's largest oil field and blocked technicians from reaching it, sharply cutting Sharara output.

26 Sep — Zawiya: The NOC shut a refining unit at the Zawiya refinery because of the continued forced closure, reporting about 942,000 barrels of lost output and about $95 million in losses over five days; PFG members also blocked the refinery gates.
26 Sep — Tripoli: UNSMIL expressed concern over the pipeline closure and urged all parties to safeguard the country's oil and energy facilities.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained, at the upper end of the band. Armed guard units are using oil infrastructure as coercive leverage, with repeated valve closures, a blockaded refinery and losses of nearly $100 million. Together with the dismantled drone-sabotage cell that targeted energy sites in Tripoli and Zawiya, reports linking a Haftar son to drone attacks, and eastern extrajudicial killings, this points to sustained armed pressure on the state, but without open fighting this week. Over the next 90 days, expect more pipeline and refinery shutdowns and possible NOC force majeure declarations, with a plausible risk of limited armed clashes in Zawiya or Tripoli, which would justify HIGH. The US-backed unity effort is in doubt, and a return to full-scale war remains unlikely.

countries.name: Tunisia
incidents: 20 Sep — Tunis: Demonstrators marched to demand the release of four jailed Global Sumud Flotilla organisers (Wael Nouar, Nabil Chennoufi, Ghassan Boughediri and Ghassan Hanchiri), held since March on fund-misuse charges, as Nouar's hunger strike entered its second month.
20–21 Sep — Tunis: Authorities detained between 11 and 15 participants after the protest, extending President Saied's crackdown on activists, journalists and opposition figures.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. No new significant security incident was found for 25 September–8 October; the most recent developments are the flotilla protest and the arrests that followed. Tunisia still fits MODERATE: repression and protests with limited violence and no organised armed threat. Over the next 90 days, the main trigger for wider unrest is the health of the jailed hunger strikers; a death or medical collapse could spark larger demonstrations. Expect continued arrests under the 'false news' decree and financial-crime charges, persistent anger over economic conditions and shortages, and secondary risk from instability in western Libya along the border.

regions.name: Ukraine/Russia
overview: Russia has opened a new phase of its strike campaign against Ukrainian cities: since 1 October it has hit Kyiv's Dnipro bridges (Southern, Paton and Northern) for the first time in the war, and on 7 October it launched a combined attack of 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles and ballistic missiles that killed at least 20 people, 14 of them in a single apartment block in Pryluky. Zelensky says Russia is following a 'new doctrine' of hitting civilian infrastructure to push people out of the cities.

Ukraine is matching this with deep strikes on Russian energy. On 2 October it hit the Volgograd refinery and Europe's largest oil tank farm in Samara, on 5–6 October an oil pumping and dispatch station in Moscow Oblast, and on 7 October oil facilities in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions. Both sides have said they will step up long-range attacks.

Diplomacy is moving, but only on paper. The US is pushing three steps: a reciprocal energy ceasefire, reopening the Black Sea grain corridor, and technical-level trilateral talks, possibly in Abu Dhabi, by the end of October. Kyiv said on 4 October that it is ready. Moscow calls the energy truce 'a good idea' but has not committed to it, and the scale of the 7 October strike points against a deal before winter.

On the periphery, spillover and hybrid pressure continue without open hostilities. Three drone incursions on 30 September forced Moldova to close parts of its airspace, and one drone exploded near Hîrbovăț. CSTO contingents are moving into Belarus for drills on 12–16 October. Georgia's Constitutional Court has moved the five-party opposition ban case to its full bench. On the Armenia–Azerbaijan border, an Azerbaijani soldier crossed into Syunik and wounded civilians, a reminder of how fragile the unsigned peace deal still is.

countries.name: Ukraine
incidents: 1 Oct — Nationwide: Russia launched 107 drones (63 of them jet-powered), killing at least 6 and injuring 38 across Sumy, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, Kherson and other oblasts and causing power cuts. In Kyiv, drones hit a school, a nuclear research institute and the Southern Bridge.

2–3 Oct — Kyiv: Russian drones struck the Southern Bridge again, forcing the Southern and Paton bridges to close, and then hit the Northern Bridge. The first-ever strikes on the capital's Dnipro crossings gridlocked the city. 1 person was killed in Darnytskyi district.
3 Oct — Odesa region: A Russian attack on a civilian vessel killed 1 and injured 3 as Russia kept up its pressure on Black Sea ports and shipping.

7 Oct — Pryluky/Kyiv/Dnipro/Kremenchuk: Russia launched 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles and ballistic missiles at energy, industrial and residential targets, killing at least 20 people. A missile hit a five-storey apartment block in Pryluky (Chernihiv region), killing 14, including 4 children, and wounding 50.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect Russia to keep up and widen mass drone-and-missile strikes on the grid, transport links (the Kyiv bridges), Black Sea ports and residential areas as the heating season begins. The aim appears to be to make winter life in the cities untenable and to strengthen Moscow's hand in negotiations. Ukraine will keep up record-scale long-range strikes on Russian refineries, pipelines and tank farms. The US three-step plan (energy ceasefire, Black Sea grain corridor, trilateral technical talks by the end of October) is the main diplomatic variable. Kyiv has signed up on a reciprocal basis, but given Moscow's escalation an early, durable energy truce is unlikely. Even a partial moratorium would be fragile, and strikes would probably shift to military-industrial targets. Watch for air-defence interceptor shortages, multi-day blackouts in Kyiv, Chernihiv and Sumy, and further damage to the external power supply of the Zaporizhzhia NPP.

countries.name: Russia
incidents: 2 Oct — Volgograd/Samara: Ukrainian drones set fire to the Volgograd oil refinery and the Kaustik chemical plant and hit Transneft's Samara oil tank farm, the largest in Europe. One person was injured in Volgograd, and Samara halted public transport and used metro stations as shelters.

3 Oct — Belgorod region/occupied Luhansk: Ukrainian drone and missile strikes killed 1 in Belgorod region and 2 in occupied Luhansk, and a drone attack in occupied Zaporizhzhia region killed 1 and injured 10.

5–6 Oct — Moscow Oblast: Geolocated footage showed a large fire at an oil pumping and dispatch station after a likely Ukrainian drone strike, part of a sustained campaign against fuel supply to the Moscow region.

7 Oct — Perm/Samara/Astrakhan: Ukraine said it hit two oil facilities and a training ground in these regions in retaliation for the overnight mass strike. Russia's MoD in turn claimed it had struck Ukrainian plants producing Flamingo cruise missiles and drones.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Russia is waging an active war and its own territory, including the Moscow region and the Volga refining belt, is under regular direct attack with fatalities. Over the next 90 days the Kremlin is likely to keep escalating strikes on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure while using the US energy-truce and trilateral-talks track for leverage. It will publicly call the moratorium 'a good idea' but tie acceptance to protection of its oil exports and to sanctions relief. Ukraine's campaign against refineries, Transneft nodes and tank farms will keep the domestic fuel market under strain (export bans, regional shortages) and will test air defence deep in the interior. A Black Sea shipping deal mediated by Turkey and India is possible but uncertain. Regime stability risk remains low.

countries.name: Belarus
incidents: 7–8 Oct — Belarus: CSTO contingents from Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan began deploying to Belarus for the Indestructible Brotherhood-2026 peacekeeping exercise (Losvido training ground) and the Barrier-2026 biological-threat drill, both scheduled for 12–16 October.

21–22 Sep — Vilnius, Lithuania (most recent hybrid incident): Vilnius airport suspended arrivals for about three hours because of balloon-type objects from Belarus, which the airport called a 'hybrid attack by Belarus'. Lithuania's foreign minister said there is no reason to ease EU sanctions on Minsk.

Late Sep–3 Oct — Lithuania: Lithuania held its annual Vytis Dome mobilisation-readiness exercise, and reports from 25 September described Lithuanian drills simulating an invasion from Belarus, a sign of continuing threat perception on NATO's flank.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Re-tested against the definitions, Belarus has no hostilities on its own territory. Its profile is military activity that creates tension (CSTO drills, rolling readiness checks near the Suwałki corridor) together with low-cost hybrid pressure on Lithuania and Poland (smuggling balloons, migration pressure). Over the next 90 days, expect the CSTO exercises on 12–16 October to be used for signalling, further balloon incursions and airport disruption at Vilnius, and possible Lithuanian border closures and retaliatory Belarusian measures against Lithuanian freight. Minsk will keep its transactional channel with Washington (prisoner releases, potash) open. There is no indication that Belarusian forces will enter the war.

countries.name: Moldova
incidents: 26 Sep — Ștefan Vodă district: Border guards found the debris of an unmanned aerial vehicle near the village of Volintiri, close to the Ukrainian border.
30 Sep — Anenii Noi district: During a day-long Russian attack on Ukraine, a drone entered Moldovan airspace at about 05:43 and crashed and exploded near the village of Hîrbovăț.

30 Sep — Transnistria/Rezina: A jet-powered drone (about 400 km/h) crossed Transnistria near Dubăsari, forcing Moldova to close airspace over its northern and central regions. That evening a third object entered from Ukraine's Vinnytsia region and flew over Transnistria toward Rezina.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Three incursions in one day and a drone exploding on Moldovan soil show that spillover from Russian strikes on southern and western Ukraine is getting more frequent and more dangerous, but there are still no hostilities directed at Moldova. Over the next 90 days, expect more drone incursions and debris during Russian mass attacks, which may prompt calls for better air surveillance and air defence from Romania and the EU. A Transnistrian winter energy squeeze remains possible if gas reserve targets are missed, and Moscow could exploit it politically. Russian influence operations aimed at slowing EU accession, and the use of Russian citizenship for Transnistrians for recruitment, remain the main hybrid risks.

countries.name: Georgia
incidents: 6 Oct — Tbilisi: The Constitutional Court began considering Georgian Dream's lawsuit to dissolve five opposition parties (UNM, Coalition for Change, Lelo–Strong Georgia, the Federalists, For Georgia) and referred it to the full plenum.

7 Oct — Tbilisi: Ex-PM Giorgi Gakharia called the plenum referral a 'mafia-style tactic of collective guilt'. He said the ban effort is being fast-tracked and could be decided around New Year, when international attention is low.

Early Oct — Geneva/Moscow: Russia asked to move the Geneva International Discussions on Abkhazia and South Ossetia to a 'more neutral' location, putting pressure on the only standing conflict-resolution format.
1 Oct — Tbilisi: An Armenian citizen was detained for allegedly damaging a bust of former Azerbaijani President Heydar Aliyev.
countries.coa: MODERATE (downgraded from HIGH). Over the next 90 days, expect Georgian Dream to push the party-ban case through the reshaped Constitutional Court, with a ruling possibly timed for the year-end holidays. Expect continued prosecutions of opposition figures, journalists and protesters, and further restrictions on NGOs and foreign funding, which will widen the rift with the EU and the Council of Europe. Daily protests continue, but at low intensity and without significant violence. An actual ruling banning the main opposition parties is the most likely trigger for renewed mass and possibly violent unrest. That would justify a return to HIGH. Russia's push to relocate the Geneva talks adds pressure on the occupied territories, but there is no sign of military escalation.

countries.name: Armenia
incidents: 2 Oct — Syunik: Armenia opened criminal proceedings against an Azerbaijani soldier who crossed the border and shot a local woman in the leg; two children were also injured.

6 Oct — Yerevan: PM Pashinyan dismissed the deputy director of the National Security Service, Davit Sanamyan. A scuffle in parliament led to accusations of bias against Speaker Ruben Rubinyan, a sign of rising domestic political tension.
6 Oct — Yerevan: The infrastructure minister and a Turkish delegation discussed restoring the Gyumri–Kars power line, a continuation of Armenia–Turkey normalisation.
countries.coa: MODERATE (downgraded from HIGH). Over the next 90 days, expect Armenia to keep moving away from Moscow toward the US and EU and to keep normalising with Turkey. This raises the risk of Russian economic retaliation and influence operations. The peace track with Azerbaijan is intact but fragile: the treaty is unsigned, TRIPP has slipped to 2027, and incidents such as the 2 October border shooting and the heritage dispute can flare quickly. Armenian intelligence itself has assessed war with Azerbaijan in 2026 as highly unlikely. Domestically, the Pashinyan–Church confrontation, changes in the security services and polarisation in parliament ahead of the 2026 election cycle are the main sources of instability. Watch for whether the detained-soldier case escalates into a prisoner dispute with Baku, and for any further border shootings.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
incidents: 2 Oct — Armenian border (Syunik): An Azerbaijani soldier who crossed into Armenia and wounded a woman and two children is now detained and facing Armenian criminal charges, creating a new prisoner dispute between Baku and Yerevan.
1 Oct — Tbilisi, Georgia: Georgian police detained an Armenian citizen for allegedly damaging a bust of Heydar Aliyev, a sensitive symbol for Baku amid the heritage dispute with Armenia.
Early Oct — Baku: A report found that 44 Azerbaijani soldiers have died in non-combat incidents so far in 2026, renewing scrutiny of conditions in the armed forces.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There are no hostilities on Azerbaijani territory, but friction with Armenia continues: the heritage dispute has frozen civil-society contacts, the peace treaty is unsigned, TRIPP is delayed to 2027, and the detained-soldier case gives both sides a new grievance. With Iran, Baku's alignment with US aviation sanctions and its ties with Israel are likely to draw rhetorical and possibly economic retaliation from Tehran. Over the next 90 days, expect a slow peace track with periodic rhetorical flare-ups, continued Russia–Azerbaijan normalisation, and sustained pressure on domestic critics. A pattern of border shootings with Armenia or a sharp escalation with Iran would warrant a review toward HIGH.

regions.name: Sahel
overview: Mali's junta has scored its most significant northern gain since April: on 6 October the Tuareg FLA announced a 'strategic and controlled withdrawal' from Kidal under sustained Africa Corps air pressure and Malian troops entered without resistance; however, JNIM's September garrison assaults (Dioura, with sources citing up to 130 soldiers killed and 100+ captured) show the jihadist threat to central and western Mali is undiminished.

Islamic State Sahel Province has re-asserted itself in western Niger, claiming two attacks in the week of 23–26 September near Abala-Filingué and Birni-N'Konni that killed more than 50 gendarmes and soldiers, while in Burkina Faso a deadly JNIM–IS Sahel turf war and continued JNIM capture of army/VDP posts unfold largely behind an information blackout.

Sudan's Kordofan front remains the region's most intense conventional war: SAF claimed the capture of al-Mazroub, the RSF's largest North Kordofan stronghold, on 2 October, while RSF drone strikes on El Obeid (1 Oct), Dilling (2 Oct) and Damazin (7 Oct) keep civilian casualties high; refugee arrivals into eastern Chad surged to roughly 400 a day in late September.

Re-grading against the country-specific definitions: Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, Sudan and Nigeria (where ISWAP launched a four-pronged assault on a special forces base in Kukawa on 6 October) remain in active armed conflict; Chad and Mauritania are downgraded because their elevated levels rested largely on proximity to the Sudanese and Malian wars rather than ongoing hostilities on their own territory.

countries.name: Mali
incidents: 6 Oct — Kidal: The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) announced a 'strategic and controlled withdrawal' from Kidal, which it had held since the April JNIM/FLA offensive, citing the 'disproportionate use of aerial assets' by Russia's Africa Corps; the FLA called the pullout temporary.

6–7 Oct — Kidal: Malian troops entered the town ahead of schedule and without resistance after an air-ground campaign supported by Africa Corps, and the army said it had consolidated its positions — the junta's first recapture of Kidal since losing it in April.

21 Sep (follow-up) — Dioura/Sévaré, central Mali: Reuters sources raised the toll of JNIM's 10 September Dioura camp assault to as many as 130 soldiers killed and more than 100 taken hostage; JNIM also claimed to have struck air-defence systems at Sévaré airport.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days the junta will likely exploit the Kidal recapture for propaganda and push Africa Corps-backed air-ground operations further into the Kidal and Tessalit areas, while the FLA reverts to hit-and-run attacks and IEDs in the north; reprisals against civilians and renewed displacement toward Algeria and Mauritania are a realistic possibility. JNIM — not the FLA — remains the main threat: expect continued fuel-blockade interdiction on the Kayes and Sikasso corridors, further large-scale assaults on isolated central and western garrisons on the Dioura model, stand-off drone strikes on Sévaré and other hubs, and exploitation of captured soldiers for leverage. Escorted mass convoys can keep Bamako supplied, but the state will not regain control of the countryside, and heavy losses keep the risk of internal military discontent elevated.

countries.name: Niger
incidents: c. 23 Sep — near Abala-Filingué, Tillabéri region: Jihadists ambushed a convoy of gendarmes, part of two attacks that together killed more than 50 security-force members according to security sources.

26 Sep — Birni-N'Konni area, Tahoua region: An attack killed more than 30 soldiers; Islamic State Sahel Province claimed both this attack and the Abala-Filingué ambush in two statements on 27 Sep (per SITE Intelligence Group).

Ongoing — Niamey: The post-coup-attempt purge continues under new chief of staff Brig. Gen. Mamane Sani Kiaou, with the junta relying on Russia's Africa Corps for regime protection while ISSP escalates in Tillabéri and attacks spread toward the Tahoua and Dosso border areas.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. ISSP's twin mass-casualty attacks confirm a high and rising tempo in western Niger, and over the next 90 days further ambushes on gendarmerie and army convoys in Tillabéri (Ouallam, Abala, Filingué) and attacks along the Nigeria border corridor around Birni-N'Konni are likely, alongside JNIM activity toward Dosso and the Benin border. The junta will almost certainly keep prioritising regime security — purges, nationality-stripping and prosecution of critics — over counter-insurgency, which keeps grievances within the officer corps high and a further coup attempt a realistic possibility. Expect official casualty figures to lag or be suppressed, with claims surfacing via ISSP propaganda and anonymous security sources.

countries.name: Burkina Faso
incidents: 24 Sep–8 Oct — Nationwide: No independently verified, dated attack was located in wire services for this window; the junta's information blackout persists and should be read as an information vacuum, not calm.

17–18 Sep — Houet and Yatenga provinces: JNIM took control of a VDP militia post near Bobo-Dioulasso (17 Sep) and an army/VDP post in Aoréma (18 Sep), after overrunning an army detachment at Kassoum on 9 Sep and claiming the Kokorowe post mid-September.

Early Sep (claimed 10 Sep) — Kacham area, Burkina–Mali border: JNIM and IS Sahel fought one of their deadliest clashes to date; IS Sahel claimed to have killed more than 200 JNIM fighters, while JNIM acknowledged dozens of fatalities and called the claim exaggerated.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The JNIM–IS Sahel contest for Liptako-Gourma, together with JNIM's continuing seizure of army and VDP posts as far south-west as the Bobo-Dioulasso area, indicates sustained high-tempo conflict over the next 90 days, with large garrison assaults on the Mali model likely and sieges of Djibo, Sebba and Titao continuing. Government claims of gains should be treated with caution given the blackout. Analysts should rely on proxy indicators — jihadist claims, displacement data, and cross-border reporting from Mali, Niger, Ghana, Togo and Benin — and watch for JNIM pressure in the East and Boucle du Mouhoun regions and any signs of instability in Ouagadougou.

countries.name: Sudan
incidents: 1 Oct — El Obeid, North Kordofan: RSF drones struck a dormitory at Kordofan University, killing at least 5 civilians and injuring 47.

2 Oct — Al-Mazroub, North Kordofan: SAF said it captured al-Mazroub, described as the RSF's largest stronghold in North Kordofan and a link between North and West Kordofan, after fierce battles that inflicted casualties and heavy vehicle losses on the RSF; no RSF response was reported.

2 Oct — Dilling, South Kordofan: RSF drone strikes on the El Tomat, El Malikiyah and El Ma'asir neighbourhoods killed 4 civilians, including a child and a woman, according to the Sudan Doctors Network.
7 Oct — Damazin, Blue Nile: A drone strike on homes and a mosque in the Hijra neighbourhood killed at least 4 women and wounded dozens; Emergency Lawyers blamed the RSF.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The fall of al-Mazroub gives SAF momentum on the Forty Days Road corridor and threatens RSF supply lines between Darfur and Kordofan; over the next 90 days SAF is likely to push west toward West Kordofan while the RSF responds with long-range drone strikes on El Obeid, Dilling, Kadugli and the Blue Nile, and with raids on markets and mining sites. The spread of RSF drone strikes to Damazin shows the war's geographic reach is widening rather than narrowing. A US-backed humanitarian truce remains unlikely in the near term; expect continued high civilian casualties, accelerating displacement into eastern Chad and South Sudan, deepening famine conditions and continued UN debate on an arms embargo.

countries.name: Chad
incidents: 25 Sep — Adré and Tiné, eastern border: UNHCR reported refugee arrivals had surged to more than 400 a day — about 20 times the rate of previous months — with the Tiné transit centre hosting over 4,300 people amid severe shelter and water shortages; more than 55,000 Sudanese have fled to Chad in 2026.

24 Sep–8 Oct — Eastern border: No new cross-border strike or clash on Chadian territory was confirmed; the most recent direct attack remains the 27 Aug SAF airstrike on a fuel market near Tine (Ennedi) that killed 12, after which the military alert level was raised to maximum.

Early Oct — Lake Chad basin: Cameroon announced reinforcement of its Lake Chad security response amid a renewed Boko Haram threat; in Chad the faction's last major attack was the May 2026 assault on the Barka Tolorom base (at least 23 killed).
countries.coa: HIGH (downgraded from CRITICAL). Over the next 90 days Chad will likely maintain maximum alert and armoured deployments around Tiné and Adré to deter spillover from the Sudanese war, while absorbing an accelerating refugee influx as fighting shifts across Kordofan and Darfur. Further SAF or RSF cross-border drone or air strikes in Wadi Fira and Ennedi remain a credible risk — as in March (Mabrouka, 16 killed) and August (Tine, 12 killed) — and any repeat would likely trigger retaliation orders and a return to CRITICAL. In the Lac province, Boko Haram retains capacity for periodic deadly raids on army positions, and weapons proliferation and inter-communal tension around refugee areas pose a persistent internal risk.

countries.name: Mauritania
incidents: 24 Sep–8 Oct — Nationwide: No significant new security incident on Mauritanian territory was found in this window.

2026 (background) — Mali border/Guidimakha and Hodh Chargui: Malian forces and Africa Corps are accused of killing or disappearing Mauritanian herders since the seasonal migration began in January and of incursions into border villages such as Melga and Gogui, prompting Nouakchott to urge herders not to enter Mali.

Late Aug (background) — Nouadhibou/Atlantic coast: The coast guard rescued more than 460 migrants in two operations (21 and 25 Aug) after 143 people were found dead on a drifting boat in July, underlining the lethality of the Atlantic route.
countries.coa: MODERATE (downgraded from HIGH). Mauritania has not suffered a jihadist attack on its territory since 2011 and currently faces no organised armed violence internally; its risk profile is driven by border friction with Mali and migration. Over the next 90 days, JNIM's escalation and FAMa/Africa Corps operations — including possible operations after the Kidal recapture — are likely to push more refugees into Hodh Chargui (Mbera) and risk further incidents involving Mauritanian herders or cross-border incursions, which would strain Nouakchott–Bamako relations. The EU-backed migrant interdiction and deportation posture will continue to draw human-rights criticism. A JNIM attack inside Mauritania or a serious armed border clash would justify a return to HIGH.

countries.name: Nigeria
incidents: 6 Oct — Kukawa LGA, Borno: ISWAP fighters launched a four-pronged night assault on the base of the 101 Special Forces Battalion near Lake Chad; troops supported by Operation Hadin Kai's air component repelled the attack, the army said over 25 militants were killed (14 bodies recovered), and a senior officer cited by AP put military deaths at at least 10, a figure not officially confirmed.
7 Oct — Shagari LGA, Sokoto: Police confirmed an attack by suspected bandits on communities in the area that left a police inspector dead.
25 Sep — Dantutture, Kafur LGA, Katsina: Bandits attacked the community, killing a resident and abducting two others; three attackers were reportedly killed in the encounter.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. ISWAP's large coordinated assault on a special forces base in Kukawa shows it retains the capacity for multi-axis attacks on military positions around Lake Chad; over the next 90 days further base raids, IED attacks and ambushes in northern Borno are likely, particularly as the dry season improves mobility. In the north-west, bandit kidnap-for-ransom raids in Sokoto, Katsina, Zamfara and Kebbi will likely continue despite local peace deals and rescue operations. Civil unrest over security-force abuses and pressure from the approaching election cycle add a domestic stability risk.

regions.name: Asia-Pacific
overview: The Pakistan-Afghanistan confrontation has become a sustained conflict now in its third week: after the 18 September Kohat assault, Pakistan carried out three rounds of airstrikes in Afghanistan (21, 26 and 30 September), the last in Kunar and Helmand, which UNAMA says killed 10 civilians, mostly children. Inside Pakistan, PICSS recorded 225 militant attacks in September, the highest monthly total in 12 years.

Myanmar's military is relying ever more on air power against areas held by the Arakan Army: a jet strike on Kyauktaw's main market on 28 September killed about 50 people, the deadliest single strike in months. It was followed by bombing of Rathedaung town and of displacement camps in Ponnagyun on 3–5 October, while airstrikes continued in Sagaing and Karenni.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has moved from testing to friction at the border: Seoul and the UN Command blamed recently planted North Korean mines for the 21 September DMZ blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Kim Yo Jong rejected Seoul's demand for an apology on 2 October, and on 3 October Pyongyang fired what it called a hypersonic intermediate-range missile from Wonsan, about 1,000 km.

Chinese pressure in the South China Sea has extended into the air after the Xi-Trump summit: a PLA J-16 manoeuvred close to a Philippine Cessna patrol aircraft over Scarborough Shoal on 3 October, a second confrontation followed in the Spratlys on 4 October, and Beijing accused Manila of an airspace 'intrusion'. These are the first incidents since the 18 September ramming off Palawan and show that summit diplomacy has not slowed grey-zone coercion.

countries.name: North Korea
incidents: 21 Sep — DMZ (south of the MDL): A mine blast wounded three South Korean soldiers who were clearing a route; a joint ROK-UN Command investigation concluded that recently planted North Korean mines were 'highly suspected', which Seoul calls a clear violation of the Armistice.

2 Oct — Pyongyang: Kim Yo Jong rejected Seoul's demand for an apology, denied that North Korea had deliberately laid mines, called the demand 'despicable' and dismissed South Korean offers of dialogue.

3 Oct — Wonsan, east coast: North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the East Sea at about 06:30; South Korea's JCS said it flew more than 700 km, and Japan issued alerts to shipping. On 4 Oct KCNA said Kim Jong Un oversaw the test of an 'intermediate-range strategic' hypersonic missile that hit a target about 1,000 km away.

4 Oct — Seoul: South Korea's Defence Ministry rejected Kim Yo Jong's claim that allied forces had failed to track the missile's 'special trajectory', saying it detected and tracked the launch from lift-off and that the missile was within its ability to intercept.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect Pyongyang to combine continued testing of hypersonic and intermediate-range systems with a harder line along the DMZ, where border fortification and mine-laying continue despite the 21 September blast. Kim Yo Jong's denial and threats suggest that North Korea will not de-escalate in response to Seoul's demands, and further launches are likely around allied exercises and US-ROK summit diplomacy. The main escalation risk is a further incident at the border, such as a mine, gunfire or a drone, that draws a South Korean military response. A nuclear test remains a low-probability but high-impact wildcard.

countries.name: Myanmar
incidents: 28 Sep — Kyauktaw, Rakhine State: A military jet dropped two bombs near the crowded India Market and Kissapanadi Bridge around noon, killing about 50 people and wounding 58, including children and pregnant women; the strike set buildings on fire and damaged the bridge.
3 Oct — Rathedaung town, Rakhine State: The military dropped more than 20 bombs on the town and surrounding villages, killing three people, including children, and wounding more than 12.

4–5 Oct — Ponnagyun Township, Rakhine State: Two bombs hit the Byarla displacement camp at 17:10 on 4 Oct, killing at least six people, and the Pannilar camp was bombed the next morning; BNI reported on 7 Oct that residents were fleeing en masse.

6–7 Oct — Sagaing, Karenni and the Arakan-Ayeyarwady border: BNI reported that junta airstrikes killed at least 10 people at a gold-mining site in Sagaing, that daily airstrikes continue in Karenni, and that the military suffered heavy losses in clashes along the Arakan-Ayeyarwady border.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, deteriorating. Over the next 90 days, expect the military to rely even more on air power as its ground forces lose ground. Most of Rakhine is held by the Arakan Army, and the junta answers with mass-casualty strikes on markets, towns and displacement camps, as at Kyauktaw. The AA is likely to keep pressure on the Sittwe, Kyaukphyu and Ayeyarwady fronts, while fighting continues in Kachin, Sagaing and Karenni. A negotiated de-escalation is unlikely. Further strikes with dozens of civilian deaths and new waves of displacement are likely.

countries.name: Pakistan
incidents: 26 Sep — Dera Ismail Khan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: A bomb attack killed 11 people and injured about 30; the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) claimed responsibility.

26 Sep — Afghanistan border: After drones again entered from Afghan territory, Pakistan carried out air and drone strikes on what it said were 10 militant locations in Afghanistan, its second round of strikes since the 18 Sep Kohat assault.

30 Sep–1 Oct — Kunar and Helmand, Afghanistan: In a third round of strikes, Pakistan hit Shultan (Kunar) and Garmser (Helmand); Islamabad claimed 22 TTP and 'Fitna al-Hindustan' militants were killed, but UNAMA said 10 civilians, mostly children, were killed and the Taliban called it 'aggression'. On 2 Oct Kabul accused Pakistan of sending 300–400 fighters into Nuristan.

3–4 Oct — South Waziristan, Mashkel (Balochistan) and Dera Ismail Khan: Security forces said they killed 5, 6 and 8 militants respectively in counter-terrorism operations. PICSS figures released this week show 225 militant attacks in September (259 killed), the highest monthly total in 12 years, with 131 attacks in Balochistan.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days, the Pakistan-Taliban conflict is likely to continue as cycles of Pakistani airstrikes, drone incursions and border clashes along the Durand Line, with growing civilian harm in Afghanistan and a risk of Taliban retaliation against border posts. Each mass-casualty attack in KP is likely to bring a new round of strikes. Inside Pakistan, TTP- and IMP-aligned groups will keep up a record attack tempo against police and army targets in KP, and BLA/BLF operations against convoys and CPEC-linked infrastructure in Balochistan will continue. Without verifiable Taliban action against the TTP, mediation is unlikely to produce a lasting de-escalation.

countries.name: India
incidents: 17 Sep — Majalta, Udhampur district, Jammu and Kashmir: A joint Army, J&K Police and CRPF operation in the Brattal Sohan and Khubban forest areas killed two suspected Jaish-e-Mohammad militants after they tried to break the cordon with heavy fire.

23 Sep — Tamenglong and Kangpokpi districts, Manipur: Fresh ethnic violence killed a 36-year-old electricity lineman while he was repairing a 33 kV line, and 24 houses were torched in Makui Khuman and Makui Thanamba villages, most of them already empty because of earlier displacement.

Ongoing — Manipur: Naga-Kuki-Zo violence has killed at least 36 people in 2026; the state government told the Assembly that 306 people had died and 49 were still missing since the conflict began on 3 May 2023 (as of 31 Aug).
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect continued lethal tit-for-tat attacks and arson along the Naga-Kuki-Zo fault line in Tamenglong, Noney and Kangpokpi, with highway blockades and attacks on infrastructure workers worsening the humanitarian situation. A durable political settlement is unlikely in this period. In Jammu and Kashmir, infiltration attempts and encounters in the Jammu-region forests (Udhampur, Kathua, Doda) are likely to continue before winter closes the passes. Pakistan's war with the Taliban and Islamabad's claims of 'Indian proxies' add a regional variable, but no direct India-Pakistan military incident was reported.

countries.name: China
incidents: 3 Oct — Scarborough Shoal, South China Sea: A PLA J-16 fighter repeatedly approached and manoeuvred close to a Philippine Air Force Cessna 208 on a routine patrol, according to the Philippine armed forces.

5 Oct — Beijing: Military spokesman Senior Capt. Zhai Shichen said the Philippine aircraft had 'unlawfully' entered airspace over Scarborough Shoal, that this 'seriously violates China's sovereignty', and told Manila to stop 'provocative acts'; Manila also reported a second confrontation in the Spratlys on 4 Oct.

4 Oct — Around Taiwan: Taiwan's MND tracked 7 PLA Navy ships and 8 'official' (coast guard and other government) ships; no PLA aircraft were detected, in line with low air activity around the Xi-Trump summit.
23–25 Sep — Washington: Xi Jinping's state visit, his first in 11 years, extended the US-China trade truce to 10 January 2027; Taiwan arms sales were on the agenda.
countries.coa: MODERATE (downgraded). Over the next 90 days, Beijing is likely to protect the gains of the Xi-Trump summit by avoiding large-scale drills around Taiwan, while keeping up and widening grey-zone coercion: coast guard rammings and water cannon, PLA air intercepts over Scarborough, 'nature reserve' enforcement and Paracels construction, and patrols near Kinmen, Pratas and the Senkakus. The main risk is an incident in which China's own forces trigger a serious-injury or fatal confrontation with the Philippines or Japan. China's own territory faces no armed threat, and its internal security situation is stable.

countries.name: Taiwan
incidents: 29 Sep — Around Taiwan: The MND reported three PLA aircraft sorties, one of which entered the southwestern ADIZ, plus six PLA Navy vessels and four official Chinese ships operating near the island.

4 Oct — Around Taiwan: The MND tracked 7 PLA Navy ships and 8 Chinese official ships but no aircraft, showing that pressure continues to shift from air activity towards a constant naval and coast-guard presence.

23 Sep — Pratas Islands: Taiwan announced it is increasing maritime patrols around the exposed South China Sea outpost, including regular deployments of larger coast guard ships, after more China Coast Guard patrols near Pratas.

Ongoing — Kinmen: China Coast Guard vessels have entered Kinmen's restricted waters at least 24 times in 2026, most recently four ships on 8 Sep, while a record $14 billion US arms package remains paused.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, Taiwan's main strategic risk is political rather than kinetic: what the Xi-Trump summit means for the paused arms package and for US declaratory policy. Expect Beijing to keep PLA air activity low while maintaining a daily presence of navy and coast-guard ships, 'law enforcement' patrols at Kinmen and Pratas and pressure off the east coast. A large-scale drill becomes likely if Taipei or Washington takes steps Beijing considers provocative after the summit. Taipei will keep pushing its defence budget (above 3% of GDP in 2027) and its drone programme.

countries.name: Philippines
incidents: 3 Oct — Scarborough Shoal: The Philippine armed forces said a Chinese J-16 fighter repeatedly approached and manoeuvred close to a Philippine Cessna 208 on a routine maritime patrol.
4 Oct — Spratly Islands: Manila reported a second confrontation in which Chinese military and coast guard units harassed Philippine government aircraft and boats.

5 Oct — Beijing–Manila: China accused the Philippine aircraft of 'intruding' into airspace over Scarborough Shoal and told Manila to stop 'provocative acts', while continuing to deny responsibility for the 18 Sep ramming.

18 Sep (context) — Off Palawan: A China Coast Guard cutter rammed the BFAR vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat during a fuel-supply mission, the closest-to-shore intentional ramming yet; Defense Secretary Teodoro said Manila is 'developing options' to deter further rammings.
countries.coa: HIGH (downgraded from CRITICAL). Over the next 90 days, expect further CCG ramming, blocking and water-cannon incidents, along with PLA air intercepts of Philippine patrol aircraft, at Scarborough Shoal, Second Thomas Shoal and nearer Palawan, as Beijing enforces its 'nature reserve' and tests Manila. Manila is likely to respond with more escorted resupply and fisheries missions, transparency publicity and deterrence measures with the US and Japan. A serious-injury or fatal incident, or a dangerous mid-air encounter, could trigger Mutual Defense Treaty consultations and would justify an upgrade. On land, residual NPA and Mindanao militancy remains at low intensity.

countries.name: South Korea
incidents: 21 Sep — DMZ: An explosion south of the Military Demarcation Line wounded three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously, during route-clearing; two were evacuated by helicopter.

29 Sep — Seoul: The defence minister said a North Korean mine would be a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement and that Seoul would 'take corresponding measures'. The joint investigation with the UN Command then concluded that North Korean mines planted on the southern side caused the blast, and the JCS demanded an apology and a halt to border fortification.
1–2 Oct — Seoul: President Lee Jae Myung urged Pyongyang to return to dialogue a day after the military's apology demand; Kim Yo Jong rejected both the accusation and the offer of talks.

3 Oct — Seoul: The National Security Council met after North Korea's ballistic missile launch from Wonsan (more than 700 km), and South Korea, the US and Japan increased intelligence-sharing and readiness.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, Seoul will keep pursuing 'dialogue plus deterrence', but the DMZ mine incident, which injured South Korean troops on South Korean-controlled ground, raises the risk of a military incident at the border, including retaliation if a further blast or provocation occurs. Expect North Korea to answer allied exercises and summit diplomacy with more missile tests and continued border fortification. Watch for South Korea's 'corresponding measures', any resumption of loudspeaker or leaflet activity, and US decisions on combined exercises.

countries.name: Vietnam
incidents: 28 Aug (continuing) — Hanoi: Vietnam's Foreign Ministry formally protested apparent Chinese construction, assessed as early-warning radar sites, on Yagong Island in the Paracels and demanded that it stop immediately; the facilities appear designed to support the expanded Chinese base at Antelope Reef.

Ongoing — Spratly Islands: Vietnam continues its own build-out, with 534 acres added over the past year (about 2,771 acres in total), artificial land at all 21 occupied features, 15 harbours and a runway of about 2,400 m nearing completion.
Upcoming — Hanoi: Preparations continue for Vietnam Defence Expo 2026 (10–13 Dec, Gia Lam Airport), with 128 companies from 31 countries registered.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Over the next 90 days, Vietnam is likely to continue a two-track approach: formal diplomatic protests against Chinese construction in the Paracels at Yagong and Antelope Reef, while speeding up its own Spratly fortification, including completion of its runway and harbours. Watch for friction over Vietnamese fishing in the Paracels and for Chinese responses to the Spratly runway. A direct Vietnam-China naval confrontation remains unlikely in this period.

countries.name: Japan
incidents: 3 Oct — Japan: The government issued alerts and warned ships to take precautions after North Korea fired a ballistic missile from Wonsan toward the East Sea/Sea of Japan; Tokyo increased information-sharing and readiness with Seoul and Washington.

22 Sep — Yausubetsu Training Area, Hokkaido: US Army HIMARS and JGSDF MLRS carried out joint live fire during Orient Shield 26 (8–24 Sep), the largest iteration yet; Moscow called the drills 'categorically unacceptable'.

Mid-late Sep — Kyushu: The US Typhon mid-range missile system took part in Orient Shield for the first time; Russia lodged a formal protest and China warned of a higher risk of confrontation. The launchers are due to move to a US base in Japan around mid-October.

Ongoing — Senkakus and southwestern airspace: China Coast Guard patrols near the Senkakus continue at the near-daily tempo seen since 2025, and the JASDF regularly scrambles against Chinese intelligence aircraft.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained; watch for upgrade. Over the next 90 days, expect China and Russia to answer Japan's long-range strike build-up (the Typhon move in mid-October, Tomahawk) with more ISR flights, possible joint bomber patrols and naval transits of the Tsugaru and Tsushima straits, while China Coast Guard presence around the Senkakus stays high. North Korea's longer-range missile tests raise the risk of overflights or impacts in Japan's EEZ. A close-quarters coast guard or air incident, or a missile landing in the EEZ, would be the most likely trigger for an upgrade.

countries.name: Indonesia
incidents: 17 Sep — Jayawijaya, Highland Papua: Aris Sanda, a 41-year-old driver from South Sulawesi, was found dead in a burned car with a rifle cartridge at the scene; the TPNPB claimed the killing, saying non-Papuans who do not support independence 'aren't welcome'.

9 Sep — Muliama district, Jayawijaya: Three civil servants from the Jayawijaya Agriculture Agency were shot dead; the TPNPB claimed responsibility and alleged they were intelligence agents, which police deny.

18 Sep — Jakarta: Human Rights Minister Natalius Pigai acknowledged that handling cases one by one cannot break the cycle of violence and called for a coordinated national response; the Cartenz Peace Operations Task Force is investigating.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect the TPNPB to keep targeting non-Papuan civilians it labels intelligence agents, including drivers, civil servants and migrant workers, as well as Freeport logistics and isolated TNI and police posts in the Highlands and Central Papua. Jakarta is likely to respond with more Cartenz task-force operations rather than a dialogue initiative, sustaining a cycle of low-level but deadly attrition and displacement.

countries.name: Thailand
incidents: 17 Sep — Hill 450, Chong Sa-ngam, Phu Sing district, Si Sa Ket: The Thai Army said a dispute over Cambodian trenches and barbed wire that may have encroached on Thai territory was resolved through liaison talks, with Cambodia agreeing to fill in the trenches and remove the obstacles.
15–16 Sep (process continuing) — Singapore: Thailand and Cambodia opened UN-backed compulsory conciliation under UNCLOS over their maritime boundary in the Gulf of Thailand.
Background — Deep South: After coordinated arson and bomb attacks at more than 50 locations in Narathiwat, Yala and Pattani on 23 Aug, insurgent violence continues at a lower, intermittent level.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Over the next 90 days, the Thailand-Cambodia ceasefire on land is likely to hold. Local disputes over trenches, outposts and landmines will recur and be handled through liaison channels, with a small risk of a shooting incident, while the maritime dispute moves through slow UNCLOS conciliation. In the Deep South, expect periodic coordinated bomb and arson waves linked to the BRN and targeted attacks on security forces, with no breakthrough in peace talks.

countries.name: Bangladesh
incidents: 3 Oct — Dhaka: The Human Rights Support Society reported 68 incidents of political violence in September, leaving 4 dead and 527 injured, most linked to intra-party rivalry, local dominance and extortion.

18 Sep — Dhaka: Crude bombs exploded in at least seven locations, including Mohakhali, Jatrabari and Malibagh, and a passenger bus was set on fire in Kafrul, Mirpur, after supporters of the banned Awami League staged a march in Gulshan-1 that police dispersed with rubber bullets.

19 Sep — Gulistan, Dhaka: Police broke up an Awami League flash procession; follow-up raids arrested dozens of activists after International Crimes Tribunal death sentences against six people, including AL General Secretary Obaidul Quader.

24 Sep — Nationwide: Human Rights Watch warned that three laws passed on 6 and 10 Sep, including the Special Response Battalion Act that renames RAB, reverse safeguards and risk a return to enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained, with an escalatory tilt. Over the next 90 days, expect the banned Awami League to keep staging flash processions and low-level sabotage (crude bombs, vehicle arson) in Dhaka and other cities, especially around ICT verdicts, met by mass arrests. The government's rollback of rights safeguards and the rebranding of RAB increase the risk of abusive policing. An upgrade to HIGH would be warranted if ICT death sentences are carried out or the unrest turns deadly.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
incidents: 20 Sep — Nationwide: Reporting highlighted a surge in underworld gun violence, with 34–37 shootings and 17–18 deaths so far in 2026; police seized 867 firearms between 1 Jan and 10 Sep.
21 Sep — Athurugiriya: Police arrested four suspects, including the alleged gunman, over two murders (17 Aug and 8 Sep); a live hand grenade was recovered from the suspected gunman.
23 Sep — Colombo: India and Sri Lanka held the fifth round of Director-General-level talks between their narcotics control agencies, on cooperation against drug trafficking in the Indian Ocean.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. Over the next 90 days, Sri Lanka's security situation is likely to stay stable nationally. Gang-related shootings, narcotics trafficking and the circulation of weapons remain the main internal security problems and are handled through police operations. Maritime anti-narcotics cooperation with India will deepen. No indicators point to renewed insurgent or communal conflict.

regions.name: Americas
overview: Colombia's armed conflict remains the region's deadliest and most technologically dynamic: official data published on 6 October count 442 explosive-drone attacks between January 2024 and 1 October 2026 (176 this year, 25 killed and 356 wounded), a FARC-dissident drone strike killed a soldier near Neiva on 3 October, and Indepaz logged its 96th and 97th massacres of 2026 in Cauca and Antioquia, already well above the 2025 total.

Haiti's international security track has been extended but remains under-resourced: the UN Security Council renewed the Gang Suppression Force for six months (to 31 March 2027) on 29 September by 12-0 with three abstentions, with only about 1,500 of a planned 5,500 troops deployed, while gangs killed at least 11 people in Gros-Morne (Artibonite) in retaliation for GSF operations and kidnappings rise ahead of the December elections.

Organised criminal violence, not insurgency, is the main driver of instability along the Pacific and Andean belt: Ecuador's third curfew of 2026 ended on 30 September with the state of exception running to 14 November while armed attacks continued in Machala and Duran, and in Peru the killing of at least three bus drivers in Lima and Callao between 1 and 5 October has pushed transport unions toward a national strike decision on 9 October.

Venezuela and Bolivia are de-escalating from acute to managed tension: Caracas released further political prisoners after a second round of government-opposition talks and Machado signalled readiness for direct talks with Rodriguez, though a first National Guard–ELN clash in Tachira points to spillover from Colombia's offensive; in Bolivia the 28 September transport strike was only partially observed and the government has reached sectoral fuel agreements, while Cuba's grid deficit of 1,800–2,070 MW keeps the island in a state of basic-service collapse.

countries.name: Venezuela
incidents: 26–27 Sep — Nationwide: At least 20 political prisoners were released after the close of the second round of government-opposition negotiations; Foro Penal still counts about 322 political prisoners, and released detainees remain barred from speaking publicly and must report to a judge every 30 days.

1 Oct (reported) — Tachira state: One person was killed and at least five wounded in a clash between National Guard personnel and ELN guerrillas, described by analysts as the first such Venezuelan military–ELN confrontation since De la Espriella took office in Colombia, signalling shrinking tolerance for the ELN on Venezuelan soil.

4 Oct — Caribbean Sea: A US Southern Command strike on an alleged drug-smuggling go-fast boat killed four people, raising the Southern Spear toll to at least 235 killed in 70 strikes since September 2025.

4 Oct — Caracas/abroad: Vente Venezuela said Maria Corina Machado is willing to hold direct talks with acting President Delcy Rodriguez to accelerate the transition; Caracas has not replied and no election date has been set.
countries.coa: Downgraded to MODERATE. With Washington and Caracas now cooperating, the risk of renewed US military action against Venezuelan territory is low, and the domestic picture is one of political tension and repression with few casualties rather than armed conflict. Over the next 90 days, expect incremental prisoner releases traded against continued short-term arbitrary arrests, pressure from the opposition for an electoral timetable and for Machado's safe return, and the possibility of a Rodriguez candidacy that would polarise the transition. The main security risk is in the border states: Colombia's US-backed offensive is pushing ELN and FARC dissident units into Tachira, Apure and Zulia, and the Tachira clash suggests the Venezuelan armed forces may begin contesting them. Upgrade to HIGH if border clashes become recurring and deadly, if repression of opposition rallies turns violent, or if US-Venezuela cooperation breaks down. Southern Spear strikes will continue in international waters without a Venezuela-specific escalation.

countries.name: Colombia
incidents: 3 Oct — Vereda Aipecito, rural Neiva, Huila: Explosives dropped by drones killed professional soldier Samuel Pinzon Barliza Ipuana and wounded another from Artillery Battalion No. 9 Tenerife; the army blamed the Ismael Ruiz front of the Ivan Mordisco FARC dissidents.

4 Oct — Santander de Quilichao, Cauca: Armed men entered a public establishment and fired indiscriminately, killing three people; Indepaz recorded it as the 96th massacre of 2026, followed by a 97th in Segovia, Antioquia, where three bodies were found with their hands tied.

6 Oct — Nationwide: Military and police data showed 442 explosive-drone attacks between 1 January 2024 and 1 October 2026 (108 in 2024, 158 in 2025, 176 in 2026), leaving 25 dead and 356 wounded; Cauca accounts for 244 of the attacks.

6–7 Oct — Inza and Popayan, Cauca: FARC dissidents attacked the El Pedregal police substation in Inza with rifle fire, and an explosive attack on a police checkpoint in Popayan's Comuna 4 wounded two officers and three civilians.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The past week again combined lethal drone strikes on the army, harassment and explosive attacks on police in Cauca, and near-daily massacres driven by territorial disputes between armed groups, which together meet the definition of a sustained insurgency with regular fatalities and territory held by armed groups. Over the next 90 days, expect continued weekly drone and explosive attacks on police substations and military units in Cauca, Huila, Valle del Cauca and Norte de Santander, with the massacre count on track to exceed 110 for the year. The De la Espriella government's US-backed offensive will likely push ELN and FARC dissident units across the Venezuelan border, raising the risk of cross-border incidents, and may provoke retaliatory attacks on urban targets such as Popayan and Cali. Watch for the rollout of the national anti-drone shield, any first mass-casualty drone swarm against an urban area, and attacks linked to the 2026–2027 regional political calendar.

countries.name: Haiti
incidents: 28 Sep — Gros-Morne, Artibonite: Gang members burned homes and killed at least 11 people, including four members of one family taking a sick woman to hospital, in reprisal after a GSF unit killed three gang members during a push against illegal toll booths; the UN Secretary-General condemned the attack, attributed to the Kokorat San Ras gang.

29 Sep — New York: The UN Security Council adopted resolution 2829 by 12-0 with China, Russia and Pakistan abstaining, extending the Gang Suppression Force to 31 March 2027; about 1,500 GSF troops are deployed, under 30% of planned strength.

1 Oct — Port-au-Prince: AP reported a rise in kidnappings, with 81 people abducted in April–June (up 42% on the first quarter) and gangs increasingly targeting senior officials and districts previously considered safe ahead of the December elections.

5–6 Oct — Tabarre and Cite Soleil, Port-au-Prince: GSF operations backed by armoured vehicles and helicopters cleared barricades and gang hideouts; two alleged gang members were killed in a firefight on Route Soleil 9, two were arrested and weapons and homemade explosives were seized.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Gangs still control much of Port-au-Prince and large parts of Artibonite, and the Gros-Morne reprisal shows that every GSF advance carries a high risk of retaliatory massacres against civilians. The six-month renewal (instead of a full year) and the force's under-30% strength mean the GSF will stay capable of local clearance operations but not of holding ground across the capital in the next 90 days. Expect further joint PNH-GSF raids in Cite Soleil, Tabarre and Kenscoff, retaliation against rural communities in Artibonite and Centre, and continued kidnappings of officials, professionals and schoolchildren. The 13 December elections are at serious risk of postponement or partial voting; attacks on electoral staff or candidates would be a key indicator. Watch for the arrival pace of the remaining 4,000 troops and for funding shortfalls flagged by the abstaining Council members.

countries.name: Cuba
incidents: 2 Oct — Nationwide: State utility UNE forecast a 2,070 MW shortfall at the evening peak, keeping many areas without power for close to or more than 20 hours a day following the 18 September total grid collapse, the eighth of 2026.

2 Oct — Havana: A protester demanding 'freedom' at the doors of the Capitolio was reported by Diario de Cuba, amid continuing localized pot-banging, street blockades and garbage burning in Havana neighbourhoods such as Diez de Octubre.
5 Oct — Nationwide: Power shortages caused an ETECSA outage that cut the Nauta internet service and Transfermovil payments; UNE forecast a further 1,827 MW peak deficit for 6 October.

6 Oct — Nationwide: Bloomberg reported that imported solar equipment, with US suppliers overtaking China, is now keeping some lights on, underlining the dependence on stopgap fixes for a grid crippled by fuel shortages under US oil restrictions.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. There is no armed conflict, but the persistent collapse of basic services (daily deficits of around 1,800–2,000 MW, cascading failures in water, telecoms and payments) and recurring small-scale protests meet the HIGH definition. Over the next 90 days, the remainder of the hurricane season and continued fuel scarcity make another nationwide grid collapse likely, each followed by a spike in pot-banging protests and targeted arrests. The regime's security apparatus remains cohesive and has so far contained protest to the neighbourhood level. Upgrade to CRITICAL only if protests become coordinated across several cities, security forces use lethal force, or state control visibly erodes; watch also for a new migration surge and any shift in US policy on fuel supplies.

countries.name: Ecuador
incidents: 30 Sep — Guayas, Manabi, Los Rios, El Oro: The third night curfew of 2026 ended as scheduled, but the 60-day state of exception for 'grave internal commotion' under Executive Decree 498 remains in force in eight provinces and three cantons until 14 November.

3 Oct — Machala, El Oro: Three men were shot dead at around 00:30 outside a liquor store at 10 de Agosto and Guabo streets, in the province where rival trafficking gangs are fighting over port logistics corridors.

3 Oct — Duran, Guayas: An armed attack killed two people and wounded several; police intercepted the getaway vehicle after a chase in which the suspects fired on officers, detaining five men and seizing four pistols.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Ecuador's violence is organised armed violence by gangs that the state treats as parties to an internal armed conflict, with gangs contesting territory, ports and prisons and killings running at more than 20 a day nationwide, which meets the CRITICAL definition despite a modest decline from the 2025 record. With the curfew lifted, expect killings to shift back into night hours in Guayaquil, Duran, Machala and Manta, and a renewed curfew or extension of the state of exception beyond 14 November is likely if homicides rebound. Prison violence in Esmeraldas and Machala and complaints of military abuses in prisons are flashpoints. Over 90 days, expect further joint operations with US support against Los Lobos and Los Choneros and retaliation against judges, prison staff and local officials after high-value arrests.

countries.name: Peru
incidents: 1–2 Oct — Callao: Public-transport driver Juan Daniel Melasquez Anca (60) was shot dead by a hitman while waiting for passengers at Avenida Dos de Mayo; police detained four suspects in flagrante.
